about: What Semitone knows about real production instruments and effects, so it can suggest the sound to use instead of pretending its own synths match them. Each entry names the instrument, who is known to use it and how (sourced), software that recreates it, a patch recipe (what to set, not a preset name), and the Semitone instrument that stands in while sketching. Never invent preset names: name a preset only when it was found in the user's own library (see libraryMatch).

libraryMatch.about: With the user's permission, the desktop app scans the plug-in folders on their computer (names only: plug-in names and preset file names, never audio) and keeps the list locally. Suggestions then say "in your library: <plug-in> → <preset>" when a name matches the recipe (by keywords such as Juno, arp, felt, Mellotron, strings), and otherwise list software to try. Nothing leaves the computer.

automationMoves.what: narrow the mix during a build, full width on the chorus downbeat
cut everything (and reverb tails) for the last beat before a new section
high-pass the kick and bass rising through a build, bypass on the drop
a gate or beat-repeat getting faster, then a mute on the last beat
reverb wet rises over the last bars until the dry sound is buried, back to dry on the downbeat
a reversed note or cymbal swelling into the first beat
send single words to a delay or reverb to fill gaps or build before the chorus
slow pan drift on secondary parts for gentle motion
fast hi-hat and percussion panning for club excitement
EQ or filter opens on vocals and guitars for a brighter chorus; closes to cool down after a peak
a band-passed intro that opens into the verse
a master gain lift (or a dip before) at the chorus
tempo drifting up or slowing at the end
vary velocity, timing and release on programmed parts
sidechain or autopan ducking to the kick
tape wow and flutter, saturation, a little top cut
everything drops out except the vocal for one key line
distortion or saturation rising through a section
a key change up for the last chorus

emotionRules.about: How a song's emotion changes automation and effects, before any producer. A section can carry its own emotion (an emotional arc). The moves come from mixing guides (sources in automationMoves); which emotion uses which is Semitone's own rule set ("c":"low"): tune by ear and from the song analyser.

euphoric.arrangement: big chorus, layers stacked, drums driving

triumphant.arrangement: drum fills into the last chorus, brass or big pads

melancholy.arrangement: space around the vocal; reverb tails at phrase ends; a darker filter in verses

heartbroken.arrangement: pull everything back for the key line

nostalgic.arrangement: older sounds (Mellotron, Rhodes, tape echo); the intro sounds like a memory, then opens up

tender.arrangement: few parts; small level rides only

intimate.arrangement: dry, close vocal, almost no automation

dreamy.arrangement: long reverbs, chorus and tremolo on keys, soft attacks

hazy.arrangement: muted top end, slow tremolo, wet guitars

dark.arrangement: low register, sparse, distorted low end

tense.arrangement: build without release until the drop; risers

sultry.arrangement: slow tremolo, warm saturation, low-pass on keys

cinematic.arrangement: string crescendos by expression, big low hits, silences

lonely.arrangement: wide empty space, few elements far apart, a mono vocal

hopeful.arrangement: chords brighten (major lift), a lift in the last chorus

anxious.arrangement: restless rhythms, a slight tempo push

vibes.about: A vibe is the setting or picture (late-night drive, old Hollywood); an emotion is the feeling. A vibe suggests tempo, sounds, effects and likely emotions.
